items.title: Palabras de apertura del Secretario General de FELABAN en la 60ª Asamblea Anual
items.summary: Durante la ceremonia de inauguración de la 60ª Asamblea Anual de FELABAN, realizada el 3 de noviembre de 2026 en Lima, el Secretario General de la Federación, Giorgio Trettenero Castro, dio la bienvenida a los participantes y destacó el récord de asistencia alcanzado en esta edición. En su intervención, Trettenero hizo un balance del momento que atraviesa la región y del sector bancario. Abordó el crecimiento económico de América Latina, el fortalecimiento de la solvencia bancaria, la adopción de los estándares de Basilea III y los desafíos de la regulación frente a los nuevos competidores. También se refirió al avance del Open Finance y de los sistemas de pago instantáneo como motores de inclusión financiera.

items.title: Palabras de apertura del Presidente de FELABAN en la 60ª Asamblea Anual
items.summary: En el marco de la 60ª Asamblea Anual de FELABAN, que se realiza en Lima, el Presidente de la Federación, Raúl E. Guizado Novey, ofreció un análisis del complejo contexto global y de los desafíos que enfrenta América Latina para crecer de manera sostenida. En su intervención, Guizado advirtió sobre el impacto de las tensiones geopolíticas, el cambio climático y el envejecimiento de la población, y señaló la necesidad de exportar más, invertir más y elevar la productividad de la región. También destacó el papel de la educación y del financiamiento a precios competitivos, y subrayó el camino por recorrer en profundidad financiera, mercados de capitales y sistemas de pago rápido.

items.title: Deep-π*: a neural network estimate of trend inflation
items.summary: Most empirical models of trend inflation treat it as a latent random walk driven by unobserved shocks, so they cannot say which economic conditions move it. Deep- π*makes the innovations to the trend a possibly nonlinear function of a large number of macroeconomic indicators, estimated with neural networks, so that Shapley values can be used to attribute every movement of the trend to the indicators behind it. Two complementary loss functions define a current trend, which fits inflation today, and a forward-looking trend, which best predicts inflation over the next year. In US data, employment-related variables were the largest contributors to the post-pandemic rise of the current trend. However, the forwardlooking trend rose earlier, with real activity, employment, and money and credit as the main drivers from the start of the pandemic, and peaked eight to twelve months before the current trend. Both trends looked through most of the movements in energy and commodity prices. The contributions of the indicators are nonlinear, with sizeable interactions between them. Re-estimated every month during the surge, the model forecast inflation more accurately than the standard UC-SV model and a random walk, and in early 2021, when professional forecasters expected inflation of 3% or less, the forward-looking trend was already signalling an increase in persistent inflation.

items.title: Elastic in cash, inelastic in repo: hedge funds in the treasury and repo markets
items.summary: The functioning of sovereign bond markets is closely intertwined with repo markets, where investors finance long positions and source bonds for short sales. We show, theoretically and empirically, how conditions in the cash bond market fundamentally shape repo rates: When demand for cash bonds exceeds available supply, arbitrageurs, notably hedge funds, step in to bridge the gap by shorting bonds and borrowing them in the repo market. These arbitrage strategies drive a wedge between monetary policy rates and repo rates, generating “specialness”. To investigate the drivers of investors’ demand for repo contracts, we obtain regulatory data covering the entire universe of repos backed by German sovereign bonds. We identify the ultimate borrowers and lenders of securities and estimate their demand and supply elasticities for the repo market. Supply, dominated by the public sector, accounts for 87% of the aggregate elasticity. Demand, driven mainly by hedge funds, is strongly inelastic: a 10% increase in borrowing costs reduces their borrowing by only 1%. Despite being among the most price-elastic investors in cash bond markets, hedge funds are inelastic in repo markets because their bond borrowing bridges the preferred-habitat demand in the cash bond market: their elasticity is inherited from their cash-market counterparties rather than being a primitive. As a result, repo rate specialness emerges as the equilibrium price reflecting demand pressures in the cash bond market, of which collateral scarcity from central bank purchases is a special case. Consequently, the same cash bond market imbalances affect both the pricing of safe assets and repos, two markets that are of crucial importance for the transmission of monetary policy.

items.title: Debt maturity and government spending multipliers
items.summary: Government spending effectiveness depends critically on how it is financed. Using state dependent SVAR models and local projections on post-war US data, we show that fiscal expansions financed with short-term debt generate significantly larger output multipliers than those financed with long-term debt. This difference mainly stems from private consumption responses: short-term financing crowds in consumption while long-term financing does not. Torationalize this finding, we construct an incomplete markets model in which households invest in short-term and long-term assets. Short assets provide liquidity/safety services; households can (more readily) use them to cover sudden idiosyncratic spending needs. An increase in the supply of these assets, through a short-term debt-financed government expenditure shock, boosts private consumption. We first show this mechanism analytically in a simplified model, and then quantify it in a carefully calibrated New Keynesian model. We find that fiscal multipliers differ substantially across financing modes, with short-term-financed shocks typically exceeding unity while long-term-financed shocks typically fall below unity. We show these differences persist across monetary and fiscal policy regimes, with important implications for optimal debt management and stimulus design.

items.title: Prewar US business cycles under uncertainty: reconstructing quarterly GDP before 1947
items.summary: Official quarterly US GDP estimates begin in 1947; earlier quarterly histories must be reconstructed using annual benchmarks and historical indicators. To investigate uncertainty in these reconstructions, this paper systematically compares specifications drawn from the literature for reconstructing quarterly GDP during 1919–1946. The comparison evaluates predictions on concealed postwar quarters and separates variation across specifications from coefficient uncertainty within a model.

items.title: FEDS Paper: Heterogeneity in Service Fee Sensitivity: Evidence from ATM Surcharges
items.summary: Krzysztof Wozniak Service fees continue to proliferate in a wide range of markets, from retail to payments, generating questions about their impact on consumer choice, competition, and fairness. This paper explores how sensitivity to such fees varies across consumers, use cases, and competitive settings, and whether it is affected by consumer learning. I am able to conduct this in-depth empirical analysis thanks to a uniquely detailed, high-frequency panel data set on surcharged ATM cash withdrawals. Results show that average elasticity estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in consumer sensitivity to service fees. I explore ways in which market and behavioral mechanisms can help explain this heterogeneity. Finally, I investigate whether consumers strategically adjust their behavior in response to service fees.

items.title: ECB perception of non-banks: a machine learning-based approach
items.summary: This paper studies the European Central Bank’s (ECB) perception of non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) and how this perception is publicly communicated. We construct a perception index based on ECB speeches over the period 1998–2025. Sentiment in references to non-banks is classified by a large language model that we fine-tune on our own hand-labeled dataset constructed for this purpose. The resulting index reveals a predominantly negative and declining perception over time, particularly since the Global Financial Crisis. Negative sentiment is primarily associated with concerns related to financial stability and regulatory needs, whereas positive sentiment reflects the role of non-banks in fostering financial innovation and supporting market functioning. The index is made publicly available for future research.

items.title: IFDP Paper: When and for Whom Does the Sovereign-Bank Nexus Matter? Evidence from Post-Crisis Europe
items.summary: Charlotte Hoopes, Pinar Uysal , and Ilknur Zer We study whether sovereign risk continues to affect banks a decade after Europe began reshaping its financial architecture. Combining daily bank and sovereign credit default swap spreads with supervisory data on banks' domestic sovereign portfolios, we show that the sovereign-bank relationship remains economically meaningful but is highly conditional. Banks with larger sovereign holdings respond more sharply to home-sovereign risk, and this amplification is substantially stronger for mark-to-market than amortized-cost exposures, consistent with more immediate recognition of valuation losses. Sovereign-to-bank transmission is stronger for less-capitalized, wholesale-funded, and peripheral banks, during periods of elevated market uncertainty, and when the home sovereign has less fiscal capacity. The policy reforms aimed at weakening the sovereignbank relationship only managed to reduce the extent of the link, but not eliminate it.

items.title: FEDS Paper: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
items.summary: Aditya Aladangady , Ricardo Duque Gabriel , and Carlo Wix We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.

items.title: Main findings from the ECB’s recent contacts with non-financial companies
items.summary: This box summarises the main findings from recent contacts between ECB staff and representatives of 64 leading non-financial companies operating in the euro area. According to these exchanges, which mainly took place between 28 September and 7 October 2026, activity continued to grow moderately in the third quarter with similar momentum expected for the fourth quarter. Growth was particularly focused in high-value manufacturing and IT services, while growth in consumer spending was relatively weak. Employment dynamics remained subdued, with many firms in cost-cutting mode. Growth in selling prices accelerated in the third quarter, reflecting rising costs owing to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, but some slowing was expected in the fourth quarter. Contacts continued to anticipate moderating wage growth, but to a lesser degree than in the previous survey round.

The effects of geopolitical risk on sovereign debt holders in the euro area
items.summary: We use confidential granular data on euro area sovereign bond holdings to examine the heterogeneous behavior of investor types in response to country-specific geopolitical risk shocks. By distinguishing investor categories and accounting for their bond holding dynamics over time, we provide an empirical assessment of how different bond holders react to geopolitics. The analysis employs country-level geopolitical risk indices of the country of sovereign bonds, and applies local projection methods to estimate the dynamic responses of various investor groups to geopolitical risk shocks. In the case of high-debt euro area countries, i.e. Italy, France, Spain, and Belgium, we examine how geopolitical risks may trigger shifts in investor behavior that, in turn, could pose risks to fiscal sustainability.

Regulatory incentives and the structure of euro area money markets
items.summary: This paper quantifies the regulatory cost of short-term money market transactions and analyses how post-global financial crisis prudential reforms shape the structure of euro area money markets and the redistribution of central bank reserves. As the stock of reserves declines with the normalisation of the European Central Bank’s balance sheet, trading in money markets is becoming increasingly important to banks’ liquidity management. As the related money market volumes rise, regulatory constraints may become a more visible determinant of trading activity and short-term rate formation. Focusing on key Basel III requirements – the liquidity coverage ratio, net stable funding ratio and leverage ratio – the paper derives stylised estimates of the marginal regulatory cost associated with unsecured and secured interbank transactions. The results indicate that unsecured interbank lending entails material regulatory costs, estimated at around 35 basis points for lenders and around 15 basis points for borrowers in the second half of 2025, reflecting capital and stable funding requirements. By contrast, secured transactions such as repurchase agreements benefit from substantially lower costs, typically well below 10 basis points when backed by high-quality collateral. These differences create structural incentives favouring secured over unsecured intermediation, suggesting that repo markets are likely to remain the main channel for reserve redistribution as the stock of reserves declines. The findings imply that post-crisis regulation has contributed to a persistent shift in the structure of euro area money markets, with implications for liquidity distribution and monetary policy implementation.

items.title: Headwind or tailwind? How banks interpret borrowers’ AI exposure
items.summary: General-purpose technologies create large opportunities but make their distribution across firms difficult to assess in real time. We use banks as interpreters of the rise of generative AI by studying lender-specific probability-of-default (PD) estimates for private firms in four large euro-area economies. As public attention to AI rises after ChatGPT, banks lower assessed default risk for borrowers in highly AI-exposed industries by about 5%. The reassessment is weaker for labor-intensive firms and stronger among lenders with pre-existing industry expertise. Yet the favorable industry-level effect is accompanied by a systematic reordering within product markets: banks reassess firms with stronger pre-ChatGPT market positions less favorably relative to their competitors, compressing the risk advantage associated with market leadership. Credit allocation moves in the same direction, with market leaders experiencing relatively lower drawn and committed credit, more relationship exits, and fewer new lenders. The reordering also predicts subsequent bad-credit events beyond banks’ consensus PDs. Internal bank assessments therefore provide a forward-looking measure of how generative AI is expected to reshape competitive risk.
